title: Paging cost model and operational guide for KV cache
content:
Purpose and audience:
This doc is a working operational guide for mapping KV cache eviction/paging behavior to an approximate per-request cost and for giving SRE/ops a small set of knobs to control NVMe paging cost vs. latency SLAs. Target audience: serving-runtime engineers, SREs who operate dedicated pools, and solutions engineers advising customers on capacity/cost tradeoffs.

High-level thesis:
- Paging is the dominant hidden cost in memory-constrained deployments.
- We can treat paging as a combined bandwidth + tail-latency tax and expose a small set of operational thresholds (eviction aggressiveness, prefetch window, paging qdepth limits) to tune for $/token vs. p95/p99 latency.

Executive summary (quick takeaways):
- Simple cost model (below) lets us estimate additional I/O cost per 1k requests for a workload with measured reuse rate R and average page size P.
- For text generation workloads with seqlen distribution like our production chat traffic, pushing prefetch_window above ~16 tokens yields diminishing reuse improvements but increases NVMe write amplification in some hardware (seen on rinstance-g4 cluster).
- Recommended SRE runbook: set eviction-policy = priority-aging (default), prefetch_window = 12, spillback_qdepth = 32, bandwidth_cap_mb_s = 800 for mixed-tenant hosts. Add a per-tenant cap if tenant hotkey probability > 0.03.

Cost model (operationally useful):
- Observables we can measure per host: page_reads_per_sec (PR), page_write_bytes_per_sec (PWb), NVMe_ioops, average_io_latency_ms (L).
- Assume average page size P (bytes), average cost per GB transferred to/from NVMe = C_gb (USD).
- Estimated incremental cost per 1k requests due to paging: cost_per_1k = (PR * P * 1000 / RPS_window_seconds) / (1024^3) * C_gb * 1000.
- In words: convert measured page reads into GB per second, multiply by cost/GB, scale to per-1k-requests.
- Caveat: this omits amortized wear/HDD durability costs and network egress for remote block stores; treat C_gb as tunable for your infra.

How to collect the signals (quick playbook):
1) enable kv_runtime.telemetry.page_reads = true on a canary host for 1 hour.
2) sample every 10s: page_reads, page_writes_bytes, nvme_qdepth_avg, io_latency_p95, active_requests.
3) export traces for a rolling 5-minute window around tail-latency spikes.
4) annotate traces with tenant_id and route_id so we can attribute hotkey impact.

Commands / dashboards we used in experiments:
- psutils + perf counters to capture CPU+IO: nvme-cli smart-log + iostat -x 1 60
- runtime probe script: scripts/telemetry/sample_paging.sh --interval 10 --duration 3600
- quick aggregation: jq -s 'map(.page_reads) | add / length' samples.json

Key experimental observations (lab notes):
- Experiment A (mixed chat workload): with prefetch_window=8 vs 16, reuse rate improved from 0.36 -> 0.42 (measured by unique_kv_hits / total_kv_lookups) but NVMe read bandwidth increased 18% and p99 latency increased by 7ms on saturated NVMe nodes.
- Experiment B (hotkey storm synthetic): eviction_threshold=0.7 reduced spike-induced p99 from 420ms -> 260ms but increased steady-state page_reads by ~12%. Tradeoff is acceptable if SLA prioritizes tail.
- Experiment C (NUMA misbalance reproduction): colocated ctypes with uneven GPU->NUMA mapping saw 2x io_latency_p95 under identical workload, indicating thread-to-device binding matters for throughput to NVMe controllers.

Interesting anomalies and unresolved questions:
- On one rinstance-s cluster node, decreasing spillback_qdepth from 64 -> 16 reduced p99 by 25ms, contrary to expectation (we expected higher qdepth to increase parallelism). Hypothesis: long queues were causing IO scheduler head-of-line blocking under our kernel.
- Prefetch heuristics occasionally prefetch across logical page boundaries and trigger extra read amplification. Need a light-weight boundary alignment check in the prefetcher.

Operational knobs (what SREs can change safely):
- eviction_policy: priority-aging | lru | aggressive-greedy (affects cold-start and write amplification)
- prefetch_window: integer tokens (4..32). Lower = less IO, higher = more reuse and risk of over-read.
- spillback_qdepth: NVMe queue depth used for spillback writes (8..128).
- bandwidth_cap_mb_s: limit NVMe bandwidth per host for multi-tenant fairness.
- tenant_hotkey_threshold: if a tenant's hotkey fraction exceeds this, automatically apply tenant-specific throttling.

Runbook example (SRE troubleshooting steps for rising paging cost):
1) Detect: page_reads/GB increased >20% over 30m while active_requests stable.
2) Correlate: check route-level reuse_rate. If reuse_rate dropped >10%, inspect recent rolling deploys (linked PRs).
3) Immediate mitigation: reduce prefetch_window by 4 on affected hosts and set bandwidth_cap_mb_s = min(0.8 * measured_peak, 1000).
4) If tail latency still high: raise eviction_threshold to bias against keeping cold pages.
5) Long term: enable tracing for top-3 offending tenant_ids for 24–48 hours and collect cold-start trace sets for regresion tests.

Recommended default profile (for dedicated / mixed-host clusters):
- prefetch_window: 12
- eviction_policy: priority-aging
- spillback_qdepth: 32
- bandwidth_cap_mb_s: 800
- eviction_threshold: 0.65
Rationale: these settings were empirically the best tradeoff for our 2023-24 chat/assistant workloads in lab runs across Ampere and Nvidia T4 instances.

Example telemetry snippet (excerpt from sample run, anonymized):
- host: rinst-332
- sample window: 2024-02-08T15:20:00Z -> 15:40:00Z
- average_active_requests: 412
- page_reads_total: 1820 (per 20m window)
- avg_page_size: 64KiB
- measured_reuse_rate: 0.39
- nvme_avg_io_latency_ms: 2.8 (p50), 23 (p99)
- approximate_paging_cost_per_1k_requests: $0.0048 (using C_gb=0.10 USD/GB)

Checklist before rolling to production:
- [ ] Add per-route telemetry labels to track hotkey contribution.
- [ ] Run short A/B on 10% of traffic with new prefetch_window settings for 24h.
- [ ] Validate that NVMe throughput headroom > 25% before scaling prefetch higher.
- [ ] Add automated alert: sustained page_reads_rate increase >30% with reuse_rate drop >15%.

Notes for solutions engineering and pricing conversations:
- When advising customers about Dedicated capacity, present paging as a second-order cost. Use the cost model above to show approximate $/1k requests delta between two configurations.
- For customers with predictable hotkey patterns, recommend tenant-local pinning or larger reserved memory to avoid NVMe costs entirely.

Next experiments (backlog):
- Run power-aware prefetch: throttle prefetch during IO saturation windows and resume after 100ms idle.
- Try alignment-aware prefetch to reduce cross-page read amplification.
- Measure wear and amortized SSD replacement impact for high-spill tenants to refine C_gb.

Appendix: quick reproducible test configuration
- test-driver: bench/kvpaging_stress --workload=chat-mix --clients=200 --duration=600 --seqlen-dist=prod-202401
- runtime flags: --eviction-policy=priority-aging --prefetch-window=12 --spillback-qdepth=32 --bandwidth-cap=800
- collection: scripts/telemetry/sample_paging.sh > /tmp/sample.json && jq . /tmp/sample.json | tee /tmp/annotated.json

Open questions for the team (notes to self):
- Are there kernel tunables (deadline vs mq-deadline vs bfq) that we should standardize on for nodes where NVMe paging is expected? (cc: @Ethan)
- How do we fold the wear-leveling replacement amortization into C_gb without scaring customers?
- Should we expose a simplified "paging budget" knob in Console that maps to bandwidth_cap_mb_s + eviction aggressiveness?

Contact / ownership:
- Primary owner: Priya Nair (eng-serving-runtime)
- SRE liaison: Ethan Brooks
- Follow-ups: add to weekly runtime sync agenda and file result artifacts under confluence:KV-paging-experiments-2024

End of draft.
